why-databases-exist.title: Why Databases Exist: Flat Files vs. ACID 8KB Pages

chapters.heading: Why CSV & JSON Files Break in Production
chapters.text: Why not store application data in a CSV or JSON file? Every lookup parses the entire file in linear O of N time, and two concurrent writers overwrite each other or leave torn lines if the process crashes.

chapters.heading: The Storage Engine Divides Disk into 8KB Slotted Pages
chapters.text: A relational storage engine organizes files into fixed eight kilobyte slotted pages. Line pointers at the front grow forward while tuple bytes pack from the back, enabling direct slot addressing without rewriting the file.

chapters.heading: Write-Ahead Logging & Multi-Version Snapshots
chapters.text: Before mutating any data page, the engine flushes an append-only Write-Ahead Log record to disk. Readers inspect consistent MVCC tuple snapshots while writers commit atomically, guaranteeing durability across power loss.

chapters.heading: Codd’s Core Insight: Declare What, Not How
chapters.text: Edgar Codd separated logical relations from physical storage. You write declarative SQL describing what rows you want, and the cost-based optimizer automatically chooses B-plus-tree seeks, hash joins, or parallel scans.

select-projection-aliases.title: SQL Logical Execution Order vs. Written Syntax Order

chapters.heading: SQL Is Written Top-to-Bottom, But Never Runs Start-to-Finish
chapters.text: Every SQL query begins with the word SELECT, tricking engineers into thinking column aliases exist right away. In reality, the database binder evaluates FROM and WHERE long before SELECT ever runs.

chapters.heading: FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING
chapters.text: First, FROM and JOIN assemble candidate rows. Second, WHERE discards rows where predicates are false or unknown. Third, GROUP BY buckets surviving rows, and fourth, HAVING filters whole buckets.

chapters.heading: WINDOW → SELECT Projection → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
chapters.text: Window functions execute after HAVING, right alongside SELECT projection where output aliases are finally bound. That is why ORDER BY can sort by a SELECT alias, while WHERE and HAVING cannot.

chapters.step: Scene 4 · Logical Order vs. Physical Pushdown
chapters.heading: The Optimizer Reorders Execution Only When Results Stay Identical
chapters.text: Logical order defines exact query meaning, while the physical planner takes safe shortcuts—like pushing a WHERE predicate into a B-plus-tree index seek before joining, without ever changing your answer.

inner-join-equi-joins.title: Equi-Joins Under the Hood: Hash Build, Probe & Fan-Out

chapters.heading: How INNER JOIN Pairs Parent and Child Tuples
chapters.text: An inner equi-join pairs rows from two tables wherever their join keys test equal. Unmatched parent rows and NULL join keys evaluate to unknown under three-valued logic and are excluded from the output.

chapters.heading: Hash Build on the Smaller Table, Stream Probe on the Larger
chapters.text: For large unindexed joins, the engine builds an in-memory hash table on the smaller relation in O of M time, then streams the larger table through in O of N time, probing each key in constant time.

chapters.heading: Joining Two Child Tables Multiplies Row Cardinality
chapters.text: Watch out for join fan-out! If an order has three line items and two payment attempts, joining both child tables directly produces six rows for one order, silently doubling or tripling your SUM totals.

chapters.heading: Fix Fan-Out by Aggregating Each 1:N Relation to 1:1 First
chapters.text: Eliminate fan-out by grouping each child table to the shared parent key inside a CTE before joining. When both sides have one row per order ID, every aggregate stays one hundred percent exact.

btree-bplustree-internal-anatomy.title: Inside a B+Tree: Fanout 500, Routing Keys & Leaf Scans

chapters.step: Scene 1 · Why Binary Trees Fail on Disk
chapters.heading: High Page Fanout Collapses Tree Height from 20 to 3
chapters.text: A balanced binary tree over ten million rows is twenty-four levels deep, costing twenty-four slow random disk seeks. A B-plus-tree packs five hundred routing keys into each eight kilobyte internal page, shrinking height to just three!

chapters.step: Scene 2 · B-Tree vs. B+Tree Key Separation
chapters.heading: Internal Pages Hold Only Separator Keys; Leaves Hold Tuple Pointers
chapters.text: Unlike a classic B-tree, a B-plus-tree never stores bulky row payloads in internal nodes. Internal pages hold only compact separator keys and child page IDs, maximizing fanout on every upper level.

chapters.heading: Seek Once from the Root, Then Walk Sibling Leaf Pointers
chapters.text: Every leaf page stores forward and backward sibling page pointers. To evaluate a range predicate like created-at between January and March, the engine descends from the root once and glides horizontally across sorted leaves.

chapters.heading: Sequential Keys Append Cleanly; Random UUIDv4 Splits Mid-Tree Pages
chapters.text: When a leaf page fills up, inserting a random UUIDv4 splits the page fifty-fifty and dirties buffers across the entire tree. Time-ordered BIGINT or UUIDv7 keys append cleanly to the rightmost leaf page.

multi-version-concurrency-control-mvcc.title: MVCC Snapshot Isolation: Tuple xmin/xmax Without Read Locks

chapters.heading: Why Modern Databases Version Rows Instead of Locking Readers
chapters.text: If a dashboard query locked an entire orders table while computing revenue, checkout writes would grind to a halt. Multi-Version Concurrency Control solves this by keeping multiple timestamped versions of a row.

chapters.heading: Every UPDATE Writes a New Tuple Version and Marks xmax on the Old
chapters.text: In PostgreSQL, updating a balance from one hundred to eighty dollars does not overwrite bytes in place. Transaction five-oh-two stamps xmax equal to five-oh-two on the old tuple and appends a fresh tuple with xmin five-oh-two.

chapters.heading: Your Transaction Snapshot Decides Which Version Is Visible
chapters.text: When transaction five-oh-one started before five-oh-two committed, its snapshot treats five-oh-two as still in flight. Five-oh-one cleanly reads Version One at one hundred dollars, with zero lock contention.

chapters.heading: Once No Active Snapshot Needs Version 1, Autovacuum Reclaims Space
chapters.text: Version chains are not free. Once every transaction older than five-oh-two finishes, Version One becomes a dead tuple. Background autovacuum workers reclaim those dead slots so heap pages do not bloat.
